newsitem.title: USA: GM faces more strike threats from UAW.
newsitem.headline: GM faces more strike threats from UAW.

text.p: The United Auto Workers union, ratcheting up pressure on General Motors Corp., moved closer to another potential strike Thursday as workers at GM's Fairfax, Kan., car plant voted to authorize a walkout.

GM's rocky negotiations over local plant contracts have led to two strikes in the past month, but the Fairfax dispute adds a new twist -- workers there already have a local pact; they're just not happy with it.
UAW Local 31 wants GM to hire about 150 more workers at the plant to help it cope with higher production of the new Pontiac Grand Prix and Oldsmobile Intrigue sedans.
The issue is the same that GM is facing in walkouts at Oklahoma City and Pontiac, Mich., as it attempts to boost its efficiency by building more vehicles with fewer workers.
Several other GM plants have requested permission to strike from the UAW's International headquarters in Detroit.

Those include some key components facilities that could cause a virtual shutdown of GM's North American operations, including a fuel injector plant in Rochester, N.Y., a catalytic converter plant in Oak Creek, Wis., and a front-drive transmission plant in Warren, Mich.
A 17-day strike at GM's brake plants in Dayton, Ohio, in March 1996 forced the shutdown 26 of 29 assembly plants and cost GM $900 million in lost profits.
The UAW wants GM to add about 600 jobs at the Pontiac, Mich., plant, which was running full throttle building GM's popular full-size pickup trucks until the walkout began April 22.

The Oklahoma City strike started April 4 over the UAW's demands that GM restore some of the 900 jobs it eliminated when it launched production of the new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass cars late last year.

The strike has forced GM to halt multimillion dollar advertising campaigns for the cars, and a strike at Fairfax could throw a similar wrench into the launch for the new Oldsmobile Intrigue, which is scheduled to start rolling into dealerships in about two weeks.
"At this time we're still talking," said Local 31 bargaining chairman Dan Mallett. "A strike is the last resort. Hopefully we can avert it."
But he said he was confident that UAW would allow the local to strike "if we need it." The UAW plans to send an international representative from Detroit next week to participate in the local talks.
A GM spokeswoman declined to discuss the dispute, saying only that it involves "issues between the company and the union that need to be resolved,"
Another strike plaguing Chrysler Corp. continued Thursday with little end in sight.
"There's nothing to report. We're not there yet," Chrysler manufacturing chief Dennis Pawley told reporters at an automotive conference Thursday.

The three-week strike at the Mound Road engine plant in Detroit, which has forced Chrysler to halt production of most of its truck models, was sparked by the automaker's decision to shift driveshaft production to an outside supplier, which the union believes will eliminate 250 jobs.

Meanwhile, Chrysler said it will call about 1,936 idled employees back to work in a Kokomo, Ind., transmission plant on Monday, along with 976 idled workers at its Kenosha, Wis., engine plant. The production is being resumed to supply Chrysler's Toledo, Ohio, Jeep plant, which is not affected by the strike and was using stockpiled engines and transmissions.
